title: The heavy four: ص ض ط ظ
objectives: Student can identify and pronounce ص, ض, ط, ظ in isolation on sight.

Student can explain, in plain English, what "heavy" (tafkheem) vs "light" (tarqeeq) means and demonstrate the difference against each letter's light counterpart (س/ت/ذ already taught, د already taught).
Student is aware that ض is documented as the single hardest letter in the alphabet for non-native speakers and does not feel discouraged by early imperfection on it.

audio.cue: ا: an open, unobstructed sound from deep in the chest cavity — no closure anywhere, just a clear open vowel
lips fully together
tongue-tip on gum ridge
tongue between teeth
ح: a strong, breathy, unvoiced friction from the middle of the throat — like fogging a mirror from deep in the throat, no English equivalent
خ: a rasping fricative from the upper throat/back of the tongue against the soft palate — a genuine back-of-throat 'kh', not softened
د: tongue-tip taps the upper gum ridge firmly — a plain, crisp 'd'
ذ: tongue-tip between the teeth, same point as ث but VOICED — 'th' as in 'this', never a 'z'

slides.heading: Heavy vs light letters
body: Mouth cavity fills up, the back of the tongue rises, and the sound gets a fuller/darker quality
Contrast a light letter you already know against its heavy twin: س↔ص, د↔ض(closest), ت↔ط, ذ↔ظ
First formal introduction of tafkheem (heavy) / tarqeeq (light) — full rule-naming is Phase 3, but the physical sensation is taught now

slides.makhraj: same point as س, but back of tongue raised, mouth cavity fuller — heavy twin of س
notes: Heavy twin of س — say س then ص back to back to feel the difference
Sound: a thick hiss, fuller/darker than س

slides.heading: Paired contrast: س → ص
slides.instructions: Say the light one then its heavy twin, 5× each pair.

audio.cue: س: tip of tongue near the lower teeth, a thin hiss — a plain 's'

slides.makhraj: side of the tongue against the upper molars — a lateral release unique to this letter
notes: No light twin in this set (closest reference: د)
Documented as the hardest letter in Arabic for virtually all non-native speakers, including many whose L1 is Persian/Turkish/Urdu — same family risk as Uzbek
Do not expect mastery in one lesson — slow, exaggerated repetitions, no time pressure

slides.heading: ض isolation drill
slides.instructions: Repeat ض 10 times, slowly, while your teacher demonstrates the side-of-tongue placement — no grading pressure, since this is documented as the hardest letter in the alphabet.

slides.makhraj: same point as ت, but full mouth cavity — heavy twin of ت
notes: Heavy twin of ت — say ت then ط back to back
A held, forceful release with a full-mouth echo

slides.heading: Paired contrast: ت → ط
slides.instructions: Say the light one then its heavy twin, 5× each pair.

audio.cue: tongue-tip on gum ridge

slides.makhraj: same point as ذ, but full mouth cavity — heavy twin of ذ
notes: Heavy twin of ذ — say ذ then ظ back to back
Even some native Arabic dialects merge ظ/ض — approximate imperfection here is normal, not alarming

slides.heading: Paired contrast: ذ → ظ
slides.instructions: Say the light one then its heavy twin, 5× each pair.

audio.cue: ذ: tongue-tip between the teeth, same point as ث but VOICED — 'th' as in 'this', never a 'z'

slides.heading: The heaviness rides through the whole syllable
body: A heavy letter also darkens any vowel sound that follows it — a light forward-preview of Phase 3's tafkheem/tarqeeq rule, kept purely sensory here
You'll test this for real once Unit 1.3 adds short vowels

script: Open with a cumulative cold-call of all 13 letters learned so far, then introduce "heavy vs light" as a felt sensation before naming any heavy letter.
Pair each heavy letter with its light twin (س→ص, ت→ط, ذ→ظ) and model both back to back 3× before asking for imitation.
Give ض the most time and zero pressure — it is documented as the hardest letter in Arabic for virtually all non-native speakers; slow, exaggerated repetitions only.
Self-audition the linked Arabic101 videos before the lesson — tafkheem quality is subtle and easy to under-teach from memory alone.
Correct on the first wrong repetition, but frame every ض attempt as expected imperfection, not failure.
listenFor: ص pronounced as plain س — loses the "thick hiss"/full-mouth quality (teaching-mistakes-assessment.md A.2).

ض — weak or absent lateral release, produced as a plain د or a "z"-like sound instead; explicitly documented as the hardest letter for all non-native speakers and specifically named for Persian/Turkish/Urdu-background learners (A.2, A.3) — do not expect mastery in one lesson, but do flag every instance for homework focus.
ط pronounced like plain ت — loses the held, forceful, full-mouth-echo release (A.2).
ظ pronounced like plain ذ — loses heaviness (A.2); note even some native Arabic dialects merge ظ/ض, so approximate imperfection here is normal, not alarming.

Watch for tafkheem "bleeding into the vowel" starting to show up even at this pre-vowel stage — if the student adds any vowel-like release after a heavy letter, check that it already sounds "backed"/rounded, not flat (A.2 — this becomes fully testable once Unit 1.3 adds real vowels).
teacherNotes.homework: In the student's notebook: each new letter (ص ض ط ظ) written 4 full rows, saying its name and sound aloud while writing, then memorized; daily paired-contrast drill (light→heavy, 5× each pair: س→ص, د→ض, ت→ط, ذ→ظ); extra 3 minutes on ض alone, no pressure, just slow repetition; cumulative shuffle of all 17 letters learned so far, reviewing lessons 1.1–1.3 too. No printed sheets.
